<meta>This page continues the poetic eulogy of famous men from the Wetterau region. It specifically completes the account of the theologian Johann Croll’s trials in France before transitioning to legal scholars and physicians, notably the Dryander family.</meta>

<page-num>18</page-num>
->EULOGY<-

You dispense all things, second to none in piety.
Here, where the great **Seine** <note>original: *Sequana*; the river flowing through Paris.</note> wanders with slow bends,
While you followed the Muses <note>A classical metaphor for pursuing academic or poetic studies.</note> diligently for two years,
Here by chance a harsh prison held you confined and oppressed.
Indeed, such punishments were never brought upon you by evil crimes,
For you were innocent; but a treacherous host
And your own pure faith placed you and your companions
In such great danger of your lives; already they were preparing
The grim punishment of the flames: <note>Johann Croll was imprisoned in Paris around 1553 during the persecution of Protestants; he narrowly escaped being burned at the stake.</note> but—miraculous to tell—
A woman saved you in such a critical moment of affairs.
Take heart, **Croll**; piety always carries its own rewards,
And it has never failed righteous men in times of adversity;
When no hope of help remained,
Present aid was sent from the starry heaven.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Nor should I pass over you who rejoice in the name of **Laelius**,
Excellent **Laurentius**, <note>Laurentius Lælius (Lorenz Lelius, 1542–1599) was a jurist and theologian who served as a counselor in Bremen.</note> most worthy of the sacred laurel
Which **Themis** <term>Themis: the ancient Greek Titaness who personifies divine law, justice, and custom.</term> placed upon you, whose faithful student you are.
Now far from your fatherland, the **Weser** [River] <note>original: *Visurgis*; a major river in northwestern Germany.</note>
Employs you as a Counselor, as does the Prelate of sacred rites in the city of **Bremen**.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;But what of those many others I should mention, whom unique **WETTERAU**
Produced, learned in herbs and the art of healing?
Until recently, there were the two **Dryander** brothers with their dear father; <note>The Dryander (or Eichmann) family were famous scholars; Johannes Dryander (1500–1560) was a pioneering anatomist and physician at the University of Marburg.</note>
What the most specific cause of diseases might be, what the medical
Arts may achieve, what power works within herbs:
What increase of virtues **GOD** Himself administers to them,
The father himself taught, as close as possible to his native shores

--- Page 573 ---
<meta>This page continues the poetic survey of notable figures from the Wetterau region. While the previous page discussed theologians and jurists like Johann Croll and Laurentius Lælius, this page transitions to the region's famous physicians and iatrochemists, specifically praising the influence of Paracelsus and the work of Oswald Croll.</meta>

->W E T T E R Æ.<-

One of the sons left his mortal dwelling,
Snatched away before his time; but the other, in a distant land,
Following the teachings of **Paracelsus** <note>Theophrastus von Hohenheim, known as Paracelsus (1493–1541), a Swiss physician who pioneered the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine.</note>
Frees the **Poles** <note>original: *Polonos*; referring to the people of Poland.</note> from diseases with great praise, in the manner of **Paeon**. <note>In Greek mythology, the physician of the gods.</note>
This man was the "Thrice-Greatest **Hermes**" <term>Hermes Trismegistus: A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with alchemy and hermetic philosophy; calling Paracelsus the "German Hermes" highlights his status as a master of secret knowledge.</term> of the Germans,
The sole Monarch in the secret power of things;
He removed all kinds of diseases with divine art,
And taught medicines for ailments unseen in earlier years;
Happy and forever blessed are those
Who keep the divine precepts of this man while healing.
There also came to the **Styrians** <note>Inhabitants of Styria, a region in modern-day Austria.</note> one born of **Vulteius**’ <note>The Vulteius family was a prominent academic and legal family in the Wetterau/Marburg region.</note> blood,
Famous in the **Machaonian** art, <term>Machaonian art: Medicine; named after Machaon, the son of Asclepius in the Iliad.</term> whose mind was smeared 
With no deceit, long known by fame above the heavens.
But you, memorable name of the **Pincier** <note>Johannes Pincier (1556–1624), a noted physician and professor at Herborn and Marburg.</note> lineage,
You well assist the **Nassau** Dukes, and know how 
To apply medical hands to the sick, when pain has slipped 
To the bones, or a dry fever consumes the limbs.
My **Oswald Croll** <note>Oswald Croll (c. 1563–1609) was a famous alchemist and physician from the Wetterau who authored the *Basilica Chymica*.</note> follows these with fortunate daring;
He has understood all things: by what secret power nature 
Acts within its hidden recess, while fire separates the strengths of things;
What power lies in herbs, animals, and metals;
When, by a wondrous distinction, 
He draws the purest seeds of things from the impure.
I myself have seen the shining **Salt**, and I have seen the rich **Liquor**,
I have seen **Mercury**, I have seen many medicines <note>These represent the *Tria Prima* (Salt, Sulfur/Oil, and Mercury), the three foundational elements of Paracelsian alchemy.</note>
Which **Hippocrates** did not know, nor the known art of **Galen**. <note>The traditional authorities of ancient medicine, whom the new alchemical physicians sought to surpass.</note>

<meta>This page continues the praise of Oswald Croll, transitioning from his intellectual influences (like Paracelsus) mentioned on the previous page to his personal travels, his linguistic mastery, and his role as a tutor and diplomat. ### ## ENCOMIUM ##

Thus far he has explained those things which **Croll** <note>Oswald Croll (c. 1563–1609), a German iatrochemist and physician.</note> himself prepared.
For in this pursuit, traveling for seven years
Through the land of **Italy** <note>original: *Latiam terram*</note> and the **French** <note>original: *Celtica regna*</note> kingdoms,
He observed physicians and traversed various cities.
From there, sharp of mind and skilled by long experience,
Instructed in various arts and eloquent in many ways,
He returned with great fluency—whether he speaks in **Latin** <note>original: *Latino*</note>,
Or **French** <note>original: *Gallo*</note>, or conducts business in the **Italian** <note>original: *Italæ*</note> tongue.
Now he has been appointed as a master of life and character
To the young **Pappenheim** <note>Referring to the Pappenheim family; Croll served as a tutor to the young lords of this noble house.</note>, with whom he was sent to the city
Where the German princes and the sacred
**Scepter-bearer of the Empire** <term>Sceptriger Imperii: A reference to the Holy Roman Emperor, likely Rudolph II, at a Reichstag (Imperial Diet).</term> had gathered. Both performed a worthy task,
So that the integrity of the boy's captive father might be known—
He whom harsh fortune oppresses and keeps far from his ancestral home.
But you, young **Maximilian** <note>Maximilian von Pappenheim (1580–1639), Croll's pupil and future Count of Pappenheim.</note>, who fulfills the measure of so great a name,
Smooth your brow now.
For the time is even now at hand when the **Emperor** <note>original: *Cæsar*</note> shall restore
Ancient honor, and recall your father to his court.
Meanwhile, your **Croll** shall lead you up the heights of **Parnassus** <term>Parnassus: A mountain in Greece sacred to the Muses; here used metaphorically for the pursuit of poetry, higher learning, and the arts.</term>—
That same Croll whom fortune recently joined to me as a dear friend
In this monastery of **Bebenhausen**. <note>original: *Bebenhusæa ... æde*; a former Cistercian monastery in Baden-Württemberg that served as a prestigious school.</note>
Oh, how often have we spent whole hours together,
Joyful in conversation and the discourse of a learned tongue!
Our talk was not of how sweet is the thigh of a **hare** <note>original: *lepori*</note>,
Nor the praise of a **wood-pigeon** <note>original: *palumbi*</note>, nor of **hams** <note>original: *pernis*</note>,
Or the fine taste of **mullet** <note>original: *triglis*</note>;
Rather, we spoke of what honor belongs to piety, and what glory is reserved for the learned.

The poet also reflects on his personal friendship with Croll at the Bebenhausen school, emphasizing their shared intellectual and moral interests over worldly pleasures.</summary>

->W E T T E R <-
<note>The town of Wetter in Hesse, Germany, the birthplace of the individuals described here.</note>

In the arts, and in the skills of the **French** <note>original: *Francæ*</note> tongue.
I attribute this to him: if I am able to discern anything
of the voices of the **Gauls** <note>original: *Gallorum*</note>, whose rules of speaking
he handed down to me. Hail, dearest **Croll**,
together with **Pappenheim**; if my songs have any power,
no day shall ever remove you from mindful posterity.

Now come, tell, **Erato** <note>The Muse of lyric and love poetry.</note>, which eminent men public 
care holds to declare civil laws to the people;
and those others who work in honest studies 
born for the common good, whom **Wetter** brought forth
from her fertile womb: just as within the walls of **Troy**
the horse, like a mountain, poured out the brave **Greeks** <note>original: *Achivos*</note>.

Among these shines forth, like the **Morning Star** <note>original: *Lucifer*, referring to the planet Venus appearing at dawn.</note> risen from **Olympus**,
that elderly man **Justus**, founder of the **Vulteius** <note>Justus Vultejus (1529–1575), a renowned professor of law at the University of Marburg.</note> line,
happy in his offspring, through whom he shall always survive
after death; both his name and his praises shall remain.
It was his care to benefit the **Hessian** <term>Cattis: Refers to the Chatti, an ancient Germanic tribe whose name evolved into "Hesse."</term> **schools** <note>original: *Lycæis*</note>,
so that the youths might have teachers both learned and pious,
who might join character to their studies, lest the wicked examples
of evil men corrupt them, or the blind license of life
snatch them away. The wild age of our time
despises such things, but a great reward for these labors
remains in heaven—a crown made from the **amaranth** <note>A mythical flower that never fades, symbolizing immortality.</note> flower.

Next to him, born from these same native fields,
sprung from the **Stadius** <note>Likely referring to the family of Johannes Stadius, a famous mathematician and astronomer, or a relative from the same region.</note> family, whom no one has traversed more 
climates of places, until he reached the **Indies**...

### ENCOMIUM
<note>A poem of high praise.</note>

To the farthest places, where a cruel race dwells, and once
not easy to look upon, nor pleasant for anyone to speak to:
who feed on human bodies, and on dark
blood which trembling limbs shed upon the racks.
They often wished to slaughter him after he was captured,
had God not turned for the better the dreadful
hearts of the men, pitying the unfair fate of the **Christian** <note>original: *Christicolæ*</note>.
Until at last, after two lustrums <note>A lustrum is a five-year period; "two lustrums" indicates ten years.</note>, he returned safely 
to his ancestral home <note>original: *penates*, referring to the Roman household gods of the hearth.</note>, and made known
lands unknown in earlier years—whether one seeks the path
to those **Cyclopes** <note>The poet compares the indigenous people Staden encountered to the one-eyed man-eating giants of Greek mythology.</note> by chance in hollowed beams <note>Canoes or ships.</note> 
or by foot.
Hence also occurs in our song, worthy of memory,
the father of the **Crolls** <note>original: *Crolliadum*</note>, a man great in the honor of old age,
who bore the five-fold bundles and the fifth axe <note>original: *fasces* and *securim*. These were Roman symbols of a magistrate’s power to punish and execute; the poet uses them to describe the local civic authority held by the father of Oswald Croll.</note>
as **Consul** in his homeland, a grave avenger of unjust deeds,
great like the man of **Arpinum** <note>Cicero, the famous Roman orator and statesman.</note> or **Mutius** <note>Mucius Scaevola, a Roman hero known for his bravery.</note> of a long age.
Fortunate old man, your fame shall never perish,
earned for you by your own virtue; rather, it flourishes
even more through your famous sons and distant descendants.
To these is added the not-least glory of the **Sylburg** <note>Friedrich Sylburg (1536–1596), a world-renowned classical scholar born in Wetter.</note> family,
than whom no one knew the **Latin** <note>original: *Latiam*</note> and **Greek** <note>original: *Graiam*</note> tongue
more skillfully; he handles books and
diligently labors over them, and publishes them for common use
purged of errors—a man born for our benefit.
Joined to him is he who, with great praise, rules 
the handed-down reins of the ancestral **school** <term>Lycæi: Referring to the Gymnasium or secondary school, named after Aristotle's Lyceum.</term>, whose name is **Mercator**...

His lineage gave this to him, and the reward will console his old age—
the study of the **Muses** <note>The goddesses of the arts and sciences; here referring to scholarship and poetry.</note>, which if anyone should come to buy,
believe me, he will never regret it, whatever his fortune may be.
   Likewise, **HENRICVS LÆLIVS** <note>Heinrich Lelius, a scholar and rector known for his work in Hungary.</note> presents himself to us.

**BOLLINGER** <note>The author of the poem, likely the local scholar Nicolaus Bollinger.</note>, whose illustrious fame
